The Largescale sucker Catostomus macrocheilus is a large-bodied catostomid native to the Pacific Northwest, where it occupies a range of riverine and lacustrine habitats. Egg diameters reported for congeneric species, such as Catostomus columbianus, range from 2.1 to 3.0 mm, and when converted to mass, a fertilised ovum of this species has an estimated wet weight of approximately 0.0082 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0082 grams] at oviposition. This modest initial mass belies the considerable growth trajectory the species achieves over its lifetime. Field surveys of adult populations have documented individuals attaining a total length of 61 centimeters [Li = 61 centimeters], though FishBase records a somewhat shorter typical maximum of 30 centimeters, suggesting substantial geographic variation in asymptotic size. The length-weight relationship derived from extensive sampling indicates that such a length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of roughly 1670 grams [Wwi = roughly 1670 grams], placing this species among the larger members of its genus.

Sexual maturation in Largescale sucker involves a protracted period of somatic growth before individuals become reproductively viable. Mark-recapture studies have estimated that the total length at which 50 percent of individuals are sexually mature is approximately 41.2 centimeters [Lp = approximately 41.2 centimeters], a size that typically corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of about 497 grams [Wwp = about 497 grams] when applying the species-specific length-mass conversion. Maturation is not strictly size-dependent, however, as environmental conditions also play a role. At a stable water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been determined to be approximately 6 years since birth [tp = approximately 6 years since birth], indicating that most individuals do not reach sexual maturity until their seventh year of life, a comparatively slow pace of reproductive development for a freshwater teleost.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified under controlled thermal conditions. At a constant water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], gravid females have been observed to produce a daily fecundity that corresponds to approximately 55 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 55 eggs per day], a figure derived from the product of clutch size and spawning frequency over a full calendar year. The thermal regime is critical, because spawning activity is tightly coupled to seasonal temperature cues; at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the initiation of exogenous feeding begins and metabolic rates are elevated, supporting the energetic demands of gametogenesis and spawning events across the breeding season.

Early life history in this species is characterized by a rapid morphological transformation following the yolk-sac larval stage. During larval metamorphosis, the growth rate recorded under laboratory conditions maintained at 14 °C [T = 14 °C] is approximately 0.02 centimeters per day , a rate that facilitates the transition from a free-swimming, exogenously feeding larva to a benthic juvenile recruit within a few weeks. This period of accelerated growth is essential for escaping size-selective predation in the planktonic environment. Following settlement, juvenile fish continue to grow steadily, though the daily increment slows as energy is increasingly channeled into tissue differentiation and organ development characteristic of the post-metamorphic phase.

Longevity in Catostomus macrocheilus is notable for a catostomid of its size, with the maximum recorded lifespan in the wild reaching approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] at 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This extended lifespan is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic maintenance over rapid reproduction, as evidenced by the delayed maturation and modest annual reproductive output. Comparative analyses with congeners, such as the bridgelip sucker Catostomus columbianus, suggest that the Largescale sucker's larger ultimate size and longer life are linked to its occupation of more productive, stable habitats where adult survival is high. The maximum length of 61 centimeters [Li = 61 centimeters] and ultimate mass of 1670 grams [Wwi = 1670 grams] place Catostomus macrocheilus among the largest members of its genus, an adaptation likely linked to the stable, productive habitats it occupies in the Pacific Northwest.
